input_signals.name: Weakest-Link Cheap And Solvent
input_signals.expression: MIN(IND_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_RANK(RATIO(SUB(ADD(re, che), lt), at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A stock is a compensated value opportunity only if it clears both hurdles simultaneously; the payoff is governed by the binding constraint, so the relevant score is the minimum of within-industry cheapness rank and within-industry solvency-buffer rank (retained earnings plus cash minus total liabilities, scaled by assets).
input_signals.reasoning:
MIN is a conjunctive, non-additive interaction that replaces the arbitrary 50/25/25 weighting of the earlier nested SUMRANK — no fixed weights are imposed and a high score is unattainable by excelling on one theme alone. The short leg is economically coherent rather than a mixture of good states: a low minimum means the firm is either richly priced or has an eroded solvency buffer, both of which carry low expected returns, whereas the earlier rank-product's low end contained attractive cheap-unlevered firms.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: min( ind_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_rank( ratio( sub( add( re, che ), lt ), at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Accumulated Deficit Flipped Value
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), SIGN(re))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheapness is a compensated discount for firms with a positive stock of lifetime retained earnings, but for firms carrying an accumulated deficit the same discount reflects capital that has been destroyed and is not coming back, so the value slope flips sign across the retained-earnings state.
input_signals.reasoning: Retained earnings is the single cleanest stock measure of whether a firm has ever generated distributable value, and unlike a leverage ratio it is not mechanically tied to industry capital structure. The bounded rank on the valuation leg keeps negative-book and outlier B/M firms from dominating the Fama-MacBeth slope, while the sign gate produces a fully populated two-sided spread: long cheap firms with real accumulated profits, short equally cheap firms with deficits.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), sign( re ) )

input_signals.name: Pretax Loss Chronicity Weighted Yield
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), SUB(TS_SUM(INDICATOR(pi, 0), 5), TS_SUM(INDICATOR(NEG(pi), 0), 5)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A high operating-earnings yield is a compensated discount when the firm has been consistently profitable before tax, and is a distressed-option price when the same yield sits on a five-year record dominated by pretax losses; the value slope should scale with the net count of profitable years.
input_signals.reasoning:
Replacing the tax line with pretax income removes the deferred-tax, valuation-allowance and carryback artifacts the critic identified, since pi is the pre-tax operating verdict rather than a book accounting accrual. The graded net count from minus five to plus five also cures the thin-short-leg problem: loss years are common enough that both tails are densely populated and the multiplier degrades smoothly instead of hinging on one noisy annual sign.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ebitda, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), sub( ts_sum( indicator( pi, 0 ), 5 ), ts_sum( indicator( neg( pi ), 0 ), 5 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Debt Capacity Coverage Value
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Lenders judge solvency by how many years of operating cash generation it would take to retire the obligations, so a book discount is compensated when EBITDA covers a large share of total liabilities and is a distressed option when coverage is thin or negative.
input_signals.reasoning:
This drops the capital-structure wedge and the retained-earnings gate entirely and substitutes the actual credit-market solvency metric, EBITDA relative to total liabilities, which is a flow-to-obligation concept rather than the stock-to-asset ratios already in the archive and is scaled by what the firm owes rather than by assets, so it is not a repackaged RMW profitability leg. Loss-making firms fall to the bottom of the coverage rank naturally, giving a monotone, densely populated multiplier without any post-hoc sign choices.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), zscore( rank( ratio( ebitda, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Binding Solvency Constraint Revenue Value
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(revt, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(MIN(RATIO(wcap, lt), RATIO(re, lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Solvency fails at its weakest point, so a cheap firm should be judged by the worse of its liquidity buffer and its lifetime earnings buffer, both measured against total obligations; revenue bought cheaply is compensated only when neither buffer is binding.
input_signals.reasoning:
The archived MIN construct took the minimum across themes, which compressed the valuation leg and left the sorted extremes tie-ridden; here MIN operates strictly inside the distress theme to identify the binding constraint, and the valuation leg enters at full resolution, which is a structurally different use of the operator rather than a re-parameterization. Using revenue-to-price for the valuation leg also moves the long side away from the profitable, conservative, high-book-to-market firms whose returns the five-factor model already spans, which is the diagnosed reason earlier healthy-cheapness signals produced positive slopes but no alpha.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( revt, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), zscore( rank( min( ratio( wcap, lt ), ratio( re, lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Realizable Collateral And Servicing Capacity
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Surviving distress requires either paying claims from operations or realizing value from assets, so a cheap firm is compensated when it has both operating coverage of its obligations and a liquid asset base, and is a trap when it has neither.
input_signals.reasoning: The two legs have complementary and non-overlapping evidence profiles in the archive — EBITDA over liabilities delivered a 2.22 slope with no alpha, collateral liquidity delivered a 4.73-t alpha with no slope — which is the signature of two distinct sources of information rather than two proxies for one construct. Equal ranking is justified because the legs answer different survival questions, cash-flow service versus asset realization, and the test is explicitly whether the joint signal inherits both forms of evidence.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), zscore( sumrank( ratio( act, at ), ratio( ebitda, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Illiquid Asset Productivity Value
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, SUB(at, act)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Collateral liquidity tells you what the realizable part of the balance sheet is worth; the remaining question is whether the illiquid part earns its keep, because fixed assets that generate no operating cash are impairment candidates and the book value anchoring a cheap stock is then fictitious.
input_signals.reasoning: Every distress channel tested so far measures either liabilities or liquid resources, while this measures the cash productivity of the non-realizable asset base, which is precisely the part of book value most likely to be written down and therefore the part that determines whether a low price-to-book is genuine. It is not a profitability ratio in the RMW sense because the deflator is the illiquid asset base rather than total assets or equity, so asset-light firms with modest earnings can rank high and capital-heavy underperformers rank low.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), zscore( rank( ratio( ebitda, sub( at, act ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Cash Yield Survival Cheapness
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(oancf, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The survival interaction should hold for any credible measure of cheapness, and operating cash flow per dollar of price is a valuation measure that does not depend on the accounting book value whose reliability is itself in question for distressed firms.
input_signals.reasoning: This isolates the valuation leg of the archive's best signal, testing whether the joint slope-and-alpha result is a property of the survival interaction or an artifact of book-to-market's factor structure, which matters because HML absorption is the diagnosed reason earlier healthy-cheapness signals lost their alpha. A cash-flow-based discount also avoids double-counting the balance sheet on both sides of the product, making the interaction cleaner economically.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( oancf, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), zscore( sumrank( ratio( act, at ), ratio( ebitda, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: One Year Liquidity Surplus Value
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(act, ebitda), lct), at), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Default happens on a calendar: what determines whether a cheap firm survives the next twelve months is whether its assets convertible within the year plus one year of operating earnings exceed the claims that fall due within that same year.
input_signals.reasoning:
This drops the rank-blend structure entirely and states the survival condition as a horizon-matched net surplus, which removes both the implicit-weighting problem the critic identified and the stock-versus-flow incoherence, since a one-year flow is being compared to one-year obligations. It is not an incremental leg on the existing composite: firms with abundant collateral but a heavy current maturity load now score negatively, a distinction no ranked-average version can express.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), zscore( winsor( ratio( sub( add( act, ebitda ), lct ), at ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Five Year Resource Stock Per Claim
input_signals.expression: RATIO(ADD(act, TS_SUM(ebitda, 5)), ADD(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A buyer of the entire capital stack should ask how many dollars of realizable resources — liquid assets on hand plus the operating earnings the business has actually produced over a full cycle — stand behind each dollar of creditor and shareholder claims outstanding.
input_signals.reasoning:
Cumulating EBITDA over five years converts the flow into a stock measured over a full business cycle, so the numerator is now dimensionally consistent with the collateral term and with the claim stock in the denominator, which was the critic's central objection. The construct is not the enterprise multiple: it is dominated by neither term alone, it rewards realized cycle-long earnings rather than a single year, and it prices resources against creditor claims and equity claims jointly rather than against equity value alone.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ratio( add( act, ts_sum( ebitda, 5 ) ), add( lt, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) )

input_signals.name: Collateral Quantity And Illiquid Productivity
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, SUB(at, act)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A cheap firm's balance sheet has two parts and each must be defensible: the realizable part should be large, and the unrealizable part should generate cash, because fixed assets that earn nothing are impairment candidates that make the book anchor fictitious.
input_signals.reasoning: This pairs the archive's largest-alpha leg with its highest-Sharpe leg, and unlike the existing best composite the two legs partition the same balance sheet rather than mixing an asset ratio with a claims ratio, so the equal weighting is economically justified as a partition rather than an arbitrary blend. The pair is untested and the components have complementary evidence profiles: collateral supplies alpha with no slope, illiquid productivity supplies slope and Sharpe with little alpha.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), zscore( sumrank( ratio( act, at ), ratio( ebitda, sub( at, act ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Broad Coverage Cash Yield Survival
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(oancf, ib), MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The survival interaction should hold on any measure of internally generated cash per dollar of price, and where the cash flow statement is unavailable, income before extraordinary items is the best available measure of that same quantity.
input_signals.reasoning: The cash-flow-yield version of the survival interaction produced the archive's best alpha and Sharpe but on only 7.9% coverage, which is exactly the diagnostic the objective warns about, so this repairs a coverage failure rather than proposing new economics. The substitution is economically justified rather than a blanket patch: for firm-years without a reported operating cash flow, accounting earnings is the same construct measured with more accrual noise, and if the result survives on double the sample the mechanism is not a small-sample artifact.

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( coalesce( oancf, ib ), mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), zscore( sumrank( ratio( act, at ), ratio( ebitda, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Blended Discount Survival Interaction
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), RATIO(ebitda, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cheapness measured on a single accounting anchor is noisy precisely for distressed firms, whose book values are stale and whose earnings are volatile, so averaging a balance-sheet discount with an operating-earnings discount identifies the truly cheap firm more reliably before the survival condition is applied.
input_signals.reasoning: Every archive entry uses one valuation anchor, so this isolates the measurement quality of the valuation leg while holding the winning survival leg fixed, and reducing measurement error on the leg that scales the interaction should sharpen the cross-sectional slope without changing the economics. It also tests whether the joint result is book-to-market specific, complementing the cash-flow-yield variant from the other direction.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sumrank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), ratio( ebitda, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) ), zscore( sumrank( ratio( act, at ), ratio( ebitda, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Market Implied Versus Balance Sheet Distress Gap
input_signals.expression: SUB(RANK(RATIO(lt, ADD(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(RATIO(lt, act)))
input_signals.hypothesis: The same firm carries two independent distress readings — the market's, in how small equity value is relative to the claims stacked ahead of it, and the balance sheet's, in how large those claims are relative to assets that can actually be realized — and when the market's reading is far more pessimistic than the balance sheet warrants, the discount is a mispricing rather than a solvency verdict.
input_signals.reasoning:
This is not a horizon or deflator interpolation of any archived surplus construct; it is a disagreement measure that only has content because one leg is priced by the market and the other is measured in accounting resources, so cheapness enters as the source of the gap rather than as a multiplicative scaler. The two ranks use different denominators, market capitalization versus current assets, so nothing cancels, and both tails are economically explicit: the top is heavily market-discounted equity whose liabilities are already covered by liquid assets, the bottom is equity the market treats as safe despite obligations far exceeding realizable resources.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sub( rank( ratio( lt, add( lt, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) ), rank( ratio( lt, act ) ) )

input_signals.name: Excess Market Distress With Servicing Capacity
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(RANK(RATIO(lt, ADD(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(RATIO(lt, act)))), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The right measure of cheapness for this problem is not the book discount but the gap between how distressed the market prices a firm and how distressed its balance sheet says it is; that excess market pessimism is compensated when operating earnings actually cover the obligations.
input_signals.reasoning: The distress gap delivered the archive's best Sharpe and a 3.35 slope as a standalone construct but only a 2.0-t alpha, which is the profile of a valuation measure awaiting a survival condition, exactly as book-to-market behaved before it was interacted. Promoting it from standalone signal to scaling leg is a structural change rather than a variant, and it replaces an accounting anchor with a market-versus-fundamentals disagreement anchor that no interacted signal in the archive has used.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( sub( rank( ratio( lt, add( lt, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) ), rank( ratio( lt, act ) ) ) ), zscore( rank( ratio( ebitda, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Industry Neutral Survival Cheapness
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: If the survival interaction is a firm-level solvency effect it should hold when each firm is compared with its own industry, whereas if it is a sector tilt toward distributors and asset-light businesses it will disappear once industry means are removed.
input_signals.reasoning: Balance-sheet composition ratios are heavily industry-determined, and the critic has repeatedly flagged that the collateral results may reflect sector membership rather than realizability, so this is the direct falsification test of the archive's central mechanism. It is a deliberate one-operator design isolate whose informational value is diagnostic: a preserved alpha establishes the firm-level reading, a collapsed alpha reveals that four generations of results are an industry bet.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( sumrank( ratio( act, at ), ratio( ebitda, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Industry Neutral Cash Cushion Survival
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(che, lct), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Cash holdings are the most sector-determined item on the balance sheet, so a cash cushion is informative about distress only relative to what is normal for the firm's industry; measured that way it should predict returns rather than merely reproduce a sector tilt.
input_signals.reasoning: The cash-based composite delivered a 5.6% alpha at t = 3.85 but a Sharpe of only 0.16 and no cross-sectional slope, the profile of a factor-hedged sector bet, and the identical neutralization repaired exactly that profile for the collateral composite. This is the diagnostic that decides whether the cash channel is a real firm-level survival characteristic or an industry artifact, and it directly repairs the archive's most conspicuous alpha-without-Sharpe failure.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( sumrank( ratio( che, lct ), ratio( ebitda, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Own History Discount With Neutral Survival
input_signals.expression: MUL(TS_RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 5), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A firm trading at the cheap end of its own five-year valuation range has suffered a specific dislocation rather than being structurally cheap, and that dislocation mean-reverts when the firm's industry-adjusted collateral and coverage say it will survive the episode.
input_signals.reasoning: Time-series cheapness and industry neutralization attack the same problem from opposite sides — one removes the permanent cross-sectional component of book-to-market, the other removes the sector component of the survival score — so combining them should isolate the firm-specific dislocation the mechanism is meant to price. The archive's earlier own-history construct was handicapped by a weak solvency partner and still produced a 1.93 slope, and it is now paired with the strongest survival score available.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( ts_rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ), 5 ), ind_zscore( sumrank( ratio( act, at ), ratio( ebitda, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Deep Value Concentrated Survival
input_signals.expression: MUL(MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The trap-versus-opportunity distinction only binds in the deep-value tail: for moderately priced firms solvency is already reflected in the price, while for the most heavily discounted firms the market is pricing a probability of failure, so the survival score should receive convex rather than linear weight in cheapness.
input_signals.reasoning:
This is a functional-form hypothesis about where the interaction lives, not another neutralization knob: squaring the valuation rank concentrates the survival tilt in the cheapest quintile and suppresses it through the middle of the distribution, which is exactly what the value-trap story predicts and what a linear scaler cannot express. Because the weighting change is confined to the valuation leg, a gain over the archive's neutralized composite identifies the deep-value tail as the source of the effect rather than the cross-section as a whole.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) ), ind_zscore( sumrank( ratio( act, at ), ratio( ebitda, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Improving Peer Solvency Standing Value
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ZSCORE(WINSOR(DELTA(IND_ZSCORE(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt))), 1), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Every successful construct in this archive is a static snapshot, yet what resolves a distressed discount is movement: a cheap firm climbing its industry's solvency ranking is repairing itself, while a cheap firm sliding down it is deteriorating even if its current level still looks adequate.
input_signals.reasoning:
This adds the missing dynamic dimension rather than repeating an industry-adjustment test on a third static base, and it differs from the archive's failed leverage-change signal in both content and construction, since it tracks the change in a firm's peer-relative standing on collateral and coverage jointly rather than the raw change in one liability ratio. Measuring the change after industry adjustment also removes sector-wide cyclical swings, so the multiplier isolates firm-specific repair and decline.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), zscore( winsor( delta( ind_zscore( sumrank( ratio( act, at ), ratio( ebitda, lt ) ) ), 1 ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Priced Distress Contradicted By Coverage
input_signals.expression: IND_ZSCORE(MIN(RANK(RATIO(lt, ADD(lt, MUL(prcc_f, csho)))), RANK(RATIO(ebitda, lt))))
input_signals.hypothesis: The compensated corner requires both conditions at once — the market must have stacked creditor claims high relative to equity value and operating earnings must still cover those claims — because only that conjunction identifies a firm the market treats as distressed while its cash flow says otherwise.
input_signals.reasoning:
Replacing SUMRANK with MIN makes the expression implement the conjunction the hypothesis actually states: a low-leverage, high-coverage firm can no longer score at the top, so the signal is not a sum of the market-leverage and profitability anomalies but a disagreement measure that requires both readings simultaneously. The bottom of the sort is also economically coherent, containing firms the market prices as safe and firms whose earnings fail to cover obligations, both of which carry low expected returns under the value-trap hypothesis.
REASONING_END
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: ind_zscore( min( rank( ratio( lt, add( lt, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ) ), rank( ratio( ebitda, lt ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Selectively Neutralized Survival Cheapness
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ADD(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(act, at)), ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Asset composition is meaningful only relative to industry norms, since a distributor and a utility have structurally different liquid shares, but the ability to cover obligations from operating earnings is an absolute solvency test that means the same thing in every sector and should not be neutralized.
input_signals.reasoning: Full neutralization raised alpha and Sharpe but cost cross-sectional slope (3.14 down to 2.34), and this diagnoses why: neutralizing the coverage leg discards the absolute solvency information that generated the slope in the first place. Applying the industry adjustment only where sector composition genuinely distorts the measurement is a substantive claim about which distress dimension is relative and which is absolute, and it is the one construct in this batch that could improve both metrics at once.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), add( ind_zscore( ratio( act, at ) ), zscore( rank( ratio( ebitda, lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Trough Survival Cheapness
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(TS_MIN(SUMRANK(RATIO(act, at), RATIO(ebitda, lt)), 3)))
input_signals.hypothesis: A single year's balance sheet can be flattered by an asset sale or a good quarter, so the survival condition that matters for a cheap firm is the weakest reading of its collateral and coverage over the recent past, which is what a creditor's covenant history actually reflects.
input_signals.reasoning: The archive's one trough-based test used a single narrow leg (oancf/lt) and failed, but the trough of the full survival composite is a different object: it asks whether the firm's joint resources-to-claims position ever broke down, which distinguishes durably solvent firms from firms whose current strength is one year old. It is the only construct in this batch with a time dimension, so it tests whether the mechanism is about a state or about the persistence of that state.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), ind_zscore( ts_min( sumrank( ratio( act, at ), ratio( ebitda, lt ) ), 3 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Rigid Claims And Coverage Cheapness
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), ADD(ZSCORE(RANK(RATIO(ebitda, lt))), NEG(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(ADD(dltt, dlc), lt)))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Not all claims can force a liquidation: suppliers, employees and tax authorities renegotiate, while bond and bank debt is enforced on schedule, so a cheap firm is safe when its earnings cover its obligations and those obligations are mostly renegotiable rather than contractual.
input_signals.reasoning:
This replaces the collateral leg with claim rigidity, a dimension that appears in no accepted signal and is conceptually distinct from how much a firm owns or earns — it concerns who can pull the trigger — so it is new economic content rather than an operator substitution. The neutralization is applied only to the rigidity ratio, whose level is set by industry financing conventions, while absolute coverage is left cross-sectional, following the selective-neutralization logic that a solvency test means the same thing in every sector.
REASONING_END

input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( rank( ratio( ceq, mul( prcc_f, csho ) ) ), add( zscore( rank( ratio( ebitda, lt ) ) ), neg( ind_zscore( ratio( add( dltt, dlc ), lt ) ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Solvency Sign Gated Value
input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), SIGN(SUB(ADD(act, ebitda), lt)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Solvency is a discrete condition rather than a continuous score: either realizable assets plus a year of operating earnings cover every claim or they do not, and the value premium should be earned on one side of that line and reversed on the other.
input_signals.reasoning:
Nine generations of continuous, centered survival scores have never tested the hard inequality as a gate, and the distinction matters economically because a firm one dollar short of covering its claims is qualitatively different from one comfortably above, whereas a z-score treats the difference as marginal. The gate produces a genuinely different portfolio — long cheap solvent firms, short equally cheap insolvent ones, with expensive firms near zero on both sides — and it needs no deflator, no winsorization and no industry adjustment, so it is the most parsimonious statement of the mechanism the archive has produced.
REASONING_END

input_signals.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(ceq, MUL(prcc_f, csho))), IND_ZSCORE(WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(act, ebitda), lt), MUL(prcc_f, csho)), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: What matters to an equity buyer is how much of the price paid is already funded by resources net of every claim, so the survival surplus should be scaled by market capitalization rather than by assets: a discount is compensated when a large share of the purchase price is pre-funded and is an option premium when the surplus is negative.
input_signals.reasoning:
Every surplus construct in the archive deflates by total assets, an accounting scale with no bearing on what an investor pays, whereas deflating by price makes the distress leg itself a valuation statement and changes the ranking materially for firms whose market value has collapsed relative to their book. This is a re-specification of the measurement basis with a clear economic rationale rather than a second refinement stacked onto a tested construct.
REASONING_END
